candidates.attacker_control: In the Spring Data web binding flow, every HTTP request parameter name becomes a property name: ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver.createAttribute binds request.getParameterMap() into MapDataBinder (ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver.java:161-162); MapDataBinder.isWritableProperty/setPropertyValue call getPropertyPath(propertyName) which passes it (with bracket expressions stripped) to PropertyPath.from (MapDataBinder.java:128-132, 205-209), and PropertyTraversingMapAccessor.read does the same during SpEL evaluation (MapDataBinder.java:255). A parameter name such as a long alternating-case or dotted chain (for which no property resolves) therefore directly drives the unbounded parse/split/fuzzy-match work. The same parser is reached from Querydsl binding via PropertyPathInformation.of (PropertyPathInformation.java:55-68).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether the snapshot already contains the MapDataBinder SpEL hardening: yes, MapDataBinder.java:180-190 uses SimpleEvaluationContext.forPropertyAccessors(...).withConversionService(...).withRootObject(map) so method/type references in parameter names are rejected, and the DATACMNS-1264 regression tests exist (src/test/java/org/springframework/data/web/MapDataBinderUnitTests.java:106-128). Also checked TypeDiscoverer.getProperty, which caches successful lookups (fieldTypes), so the cost driver is the failure/exception path, not cached property resolution. The exact upstream advisory/fix commit could not be consulted in this run, so attribution of this code to a specific CVE is not claimed.
candidates.impact: Denial of service: attacker-triggered excessive CPU work and deep recursion per request, repeated concurrently, can exhaust request-worker CPU and produce StackOverflowError on deeply nested camel-case chains; memory churn from the per-segment PropertyPath objects and repeated exception construction with large names. No confidentiality or integrity impact is shown by the source alone.
candidates.prerequisites: Application exposes a Spring Data web endpoint using MapDataBinder/ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver (or Querydsl predicate binding) and accepts request parameters; no authentication is required in the default configuration. Large/parameter-heavy requests must be permitted by the servlet container (e.g., one very long parameter name or many long names in a form/query string).
candidates.root_cause: PropertyPath.from(String, TypeInformation) parses an arbitrary, length-unbounded string (SPLITTER regex at PropertyPath.java:41/259-263) and PropertyPath.create(...) recursively re-enters itself on every camel-case split (PropertyPath.java:339 and 363) with no depth or length limit and recompiles the regex on every call (line 353). Every failed segment lookup constructs a PropertyReferenceException, whose constructor runs PropertyMatches fuzzy matching (Levenshtein-style) against all properties of the target type (PropertyReferenceException.java:52-63 and 143-150), so CPU/time grows with the attacker-supplied name length and re-splitting, and recursion depth grows with the number of camel-case boundaries.
candidates.title: Unbounded resource consumption/stack recursion in PropertyPath parsing of attacker-controlled property names
candidates.trace: Request parameter name -> ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver.createAttribute -> MapDataBinder.bind(MutablePropertyValues(request.getParameterMap())) -> MapPropertyAccessor.isWritableProperty/setPropertyValue -> getPropertyPath(propertyName) -> PropertyPath.from(plainPropertyPath, type) -> SPLITTER regex scan -> create(...) failure path constructs PropertyReferenceException -> detectPotentialMatches/PropertyMatches fuzzy match; unresolved camel-case input recurses through create(head, type, tail + addTail, base) (PropertyPath.java:362-366) until no split remains.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed: no request was executed and no timing/stack measurement was performed. Exact server-side limits on parameter name length/count (container and framework configuration) were not verified, so exploitable amplification per request is estimated from the code paths only. The precise upstream fix that later versions applied to this parser was not available for diff comparison.
candidates.weakness_type: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (CWE-400), with possible StackOverflowError (CWE-674)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned snapshot only (639 files; 623 Java sources, resources and tests). Focus areas: web binding stack (ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver, MapDataBinder, message converters), property-path parsing (PropertyPath, PropertyReferenceException, TypeDiscoverer/ClassTypeInformation), Querydsl binding, sort/page argument resolvers, projections/SpEL contexts, and the changelog/pom for version context. Read the full MapDataBinder, PropertyPath, PropertyReferenceException, PropertyPathInformation, ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver and the relevant sort/converter classes in source text; used the P1 index only for navigation (find_symbols/search_relation_facts) and verified the flagged PropertyPath matcher hint in source. Not every one of the 623 Java files was read line by line; repository, instantiator/bytecode-generation and projection packages were surveyed rather than exhaustively audited.
limitations: P1 relation index is partial: no control-flow or data-flow analysis, no semantic resolution, and 12,970 unresolved calls; index labels were treated only as navigation hints and every cited edge was re-checked against source text.
One file was excluded by the source-scope sensitive-name filter, and binary-like files are skipped; these were not inspected.
No code execution, dependency resolution, container configuration review, or runtime measurement was performed, so DoS amplification factors are code-inferred only.
The exact upstream fix commit/advisory for this snapshot version could not be consulted in this run, so CVE attribution and the intended ground-truth root cause remain uncertain.
Server-side limits (parameter count/length, thread stack size, timeouts) live outside this repository and were not verified.

rejected_leads.lead: MapDataBinder SpEL injection in request-parameter names (the well-known Spring Data Commons property-binder RCE pattern)
rejected_leads.reason: In this snapshot setPropertyValue builds a SimpleEvaluationContext restricted to a Map property accessor (MapDataBinder.java:180-190) with conversion service and map root; method invocation and type references (T(...)) are not resolvable, and the corresponding rejection tests are present (MapDataBinderUnitTests.java:106-128). This looks like the already-applied hardening rather than a live vulnerability, so it was not submitted.

rejected_leads.lead: XmlBeamHttpMessageConverter (XBProjector, default settings) could allow XXE when reading @ProjectedPayload XML request bodies
rejected_leads.reason: The converter delegates entirely to the third-party XmlBeam XBProjector (XmlBeamHttpMessageConverter.java:48-53, 90-93) and this snapshot contains no explicit parser hardening or evidence of insecure configuration; no source-level evidence of an exploitable XML parser configuration in this repository, so it remains an unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: PropertyPathInformation.reifyPath uses ReflectionUtils.findField(...) without a null check (PropertyPathInformation.java:132-133), which can throw for Querydsl paths without a matching field
rejected_leads.reason: This yields an unchecked IllegalArgumentException/error path on a developer-defined binding mismatch rather than an attacker-controlled memory-safety or privilege issue; impact is at most an error response and it does not meet the evidence threshold for a security finding.

summary: Reviewed the Spring Data Commons snapshot (623 Java files plus resources; pom version 1.13.11.BUILD-SNAPSHOT, changelog newest entry 2.0.5/2018-02-28). The classic remote SpEL issue in MapDataBinder appears already mitigated in this snapshot: src/main/java/org/springframework/data/web/MapDataBinder.java builds a SimpleEvaluationContext restricted to a MapAccessor subclass (lines 180-190), and MapDataBinderUnitTests contains the DATACMNS-1264 rejection tests (lines 106-128, e.g. fooBar[T(java.lang.String)]). The strongest remaining, source-supported candidate is the unbounded-resource-allocation property-path parser in org.springframework.data.mapping.PropertyPath, which is reachable from unauthenticated request parameters through MapDataBinder/ProxyingHandlerMethodArgumentResolver (and via Querydsl property-path binding).
